newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-OPINION-Russell Barton's Canberra Closeup-1997 agenda.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-OPINION-Russell Barton's Canberra Closeup-1997 agenda.

text.p: By Russell Barton (ABC TV Political Editor)

The crowd is hushed. Anticipation is rising as the leading political players prepare to return to the ground. But those expecting the pace of the political pitch to be faster this year are in for a disappointment.
Word from John Howard's last Cabinet meeting of 1996 -- the meeting which was supposed to look ahead to the reform agenda for 1997 -- is that the agenda is pretty slim, and deliberately so.

As noted previously, the Howard team puts everything through the political sieve which catches anything that is politically risky. By definition, reform is politically risky and it's reform that will be the casualty of Howard caution.
According to government sources, this year will see the beginning of political consolidation. The finance and business community would expect this year, instead, to be one of high activity.
Howard, after all responded to the mild criticism of late last year that the government was moving too slowly with the line that he had only been in government for eight to nine months.
It would have been fair to expect, then, that 1997 would see the pace pick up and that 1998 would be the year of stocktaking, of preparing for the next election.

The signs, however, point to a much more circumspect approach. There is, for instance, no prospect of movement on tax, despite the rising clamour from the states under coalition governments in tandem with business for a rethink on a consumption tax.
As one government insider privately summed up the prospect of more radical tax reform within the next two years: "Beazley will have to blink first."

Well, Beazley isn't going to blink. Labor doesn't have much going for it, politically, and it's hardly likely to junk one of the biggest pieces of artillery in its arsenal by suddenly supporting a consumption tax. As a result, there'll be no leadership on tax from Canberra, full stop.
That will increase frustration among the industry and social groups now forming an unusual alliance in the name of tax reform.

Ministers will continue to cite industrial relations as the cutting edge of reform. But unless there is significant progress on the waterfront there'll be widespread disappointment in business, following the government's sell-out -- as some see it -- to the Democrats on the Workplace Relations Bill.
The pressure points for the government come early. The High Court's Wik judgement is threatening to put Howard and the state premiers on a collision course.

Queensland leader Rob Borbidge has begun talks with Western Australia's Richard Court and the Northern Territory's Shane Stone to press for Commonwealth legislation to extinguish native title over pastoral leases, which the Commonwealth knows would be blocked by the Senate.
Even if it passed the upper house, it would succeed only in attracting more legal challenges for claimed breaches of the Racial Discrimination Act, which Howard promised not to touch.
This would hardly meet the goals now being repeated daily by Acting Prime Minister Tim Fischer to restore "certainty, clarity and consistency".
But the premiers are in the front line of land management and they want the three Cs delivered quickly and firmly to avoid real political pain.
The May budget is the next milestone and presents more potential for conflict.

With the economy clearly more sluggish than forecast last August, there's a legitimate school of thought that there should be only limited further spending cuts. And the Prime Minister is expected to agree, although his motivation is as much political as economic. There are, however, some in the Cabinet, the Treasurer among them, who would like to see the push for a surplus maintained.

Peter Costello also faces another premiers' conference where the state leaders will restate their push for widespread tax reform, including a consumption tax and yet another call for a fixed share of Commonwealth revenue.
Costello's last premiers' conference saw him embarrassed and excluded from the final agreement on a formula devised largely by Victoria's Jeff Kennett.

And nagging away each month at the government's credibility will be the unemployment figures. Having ended 1996 at 8.6 percent and with the employment department's leading indicator showing little sign of improvement, the excuse that the poor labour market figures are Labor's legacy will lose all credibility.

For all of that, Labor faces this coming year with little enthusiasm. Faced with a total policy rewrite leading up to next January's national conference and opinion polls stubbornly refusing to move Labor's way, shadow ministers privately admit it could be a very ordinary year.
-- Reuters Canberra Bureau 61-6 273-2730
